Part A: Intro to Structure:

, Vignettes 4, 6, and 7
Text Structure
Directions:
Today, you will think about how a story’s structure shapes what readers notice and understand. As we review examples from
Look Both Ways
, pay attention to how the opening, shifts, and ending of a vignette affect character development and reader experience.
text structure:
the way that a story’s elements are arranged and relate to each other

A very simple text structure has a beginning, middle, and end and goes in chronological order. The beginning introduces the characters and situation, the middle has the important action, and the end shows how it is resolved. In a very simple structure, the text is written in paragraphs.

But some stories have different text structures. They may have multiple points of view and very short paragraphs. They may have flashbacks and flash-forwards to tell parts of the story out of order and create suspense. A story may use text features like headings or images or include letters, journal entries, or lists as part of the story. Each of these elements can give you, the reader, a more interesting experience and help you understand the characters better.
Text Structure in
Look Both Ways

Think back to the vignettes you have read and identify any structural choices that stand out, such as lists, flashbacks, multiple points of view, or other unusual features. Be ready to explain not just what the structure is, but how it affects what the reader learns about the character.
Which of them have unusual text structures? How would you describe them?
How do these text structures affect what we learn about the characters and how their stories unfold?
Pulse Check
How does the ending of “How to Look (Both) Both Ways” fit into its overall structure?
It tells a story outside of Fatima’s list for the first time to contrast her thoughts with what actually happens.
It introduces Fatima’s list for the first time to show how the story affected her.
It contrasts Fatima’s story of walking home from school with the silliness of writing lists.
It returns to Fatima’s list to show how the events of the story affected her.

Project or display the following words where all students can see them: literal, poetry, metaphor, simile, figurative language, symbolism, explicit, implicit. Display the words in such a way that they can be rearranged, whether written on a board or shared digitally.
Say these Directions:

Look at the vocabulary words and think about how they connect to one another. As we discuss, explain the relationships you notice and how grouping the words can help you talk about texts more precisely.
Lead a discussion on the relationships that exist among these words and how they might be rearranged to show those relationships.
Ask:
What are some relationships you see among these words?

Literal and explicit are related because they are almost the same thing. Implicit and explicit are related because they are opposites. Figurative language includes a lot of other words, like metaphor and simile. Metaphor and simile are both comparisons of unlike things. And poetry is a type of writing that usually has a lot of figurative language.
Share Student Connections:
Invite students to share their ideas with the class. As students share, rearrange the words to visually represent the relationships they describe.
Connecting Words:
Prompt students to think more deeply about how the words connect.
Ask:
Can
figurative language
exist without
metaphor
or
simile
? Why or why not?
Figurative language can include other devices, but metaphor and simile are common examples that help show comparisons.
Ask:
How do these words help you better understand a text like “The Broom Dog”?
These words help me explain how the author uses figurative language and symbolism to show emotions and meaning.
Verify Meaning:
Prompt students to confirm their understanding of the words.
As students share relationships, they move words around to show the different relationships.

Help students talk about structure using precise academic language by organizing the vocabulary terms into categories (literal/figurative; explicit/implicit) and using those categories as tools for later structure analysis.
Invite multilingual connections when helpful (students can name a term they know in another language and connect it to meaning in English) to validate existing linguistic knowledge.
Require students to explain each “move” they make when rearranging words: “I’m placing ___ under ___ because ___.”
After the rearrange, have students write one “category sentence” they can reuse later (e.g., “This vignette uses ___ to create ___.”).
Add structure vocabulary early: “This word helps us describe the effect on the reader.”
“___ and ___ are related because ___.”
“___ is a type of ___, so it belongs under ___.”
“___ contrasts with ___ because ___.”
“I’m moving ___ next to ___ to show ___.”
Push students to name category relationships that will matter later: structure → meaning; literal/figurative → character perspective; explicit/implicit → reader inference.
Revoice “they’re similar” → “They belong in the same category because ___.”
Upgrade “opposites” → “contrasts with” / “functions differently from.”
If students list relationships without reasons → Prompt: “Add because + one example.”
If students confuse terms (explicit vs. literal) → Prompt: “Test it: Can a meaning be literal but still implicit? Explain.”
Students use at least one category label (literal/figurative; explicit/implicit).
Students explain a relationship using because.
Students produce one reusable “category sentence” for later analysis.

Part A: Intro to Structure:

, Vignettes 4, 6, and 7 (RL.6.5)
(10 minutes)
Introduce the idea of a story’s structure and how structure can contribute to character development, themes, and the reader’s experience.
Teach: Text Structure
Have students take out their copies of
Look Both Ways
for reference. Introduce the idea of a story’s structure, including examples of simple and complex structures for narrative stories.
Say these Directions:
Today, you will think about how a story’s structure shapes what readers notice and understand. As we review examples from
Look Both Ways
, pay attention to how the opening, shifts, and ending of a vignette affect character development and reader experience.
text structure:
the way that a story’s elements are arranged and relate to each other
Say:

A very simple text structure has a beginning, middle, and end and goes in chronological order. The beginning introduces the characters and situation, the middle has the important action, and the end shows how it is resolved. In a very simple structure, the text is written in paragraphs.
Say:

But some stories have different text structures. They may have multiple points of view and very short paragraphs. They may have flashbacks and flash-forwards to tell parts of the story out of order and create suspense. A story may use text features like headings or images or include letters, journal entries, or lists as part of the story. Each of these elements can give you, the reader, a more interesting experience and help you understand the characters better.
Display the following terms and their definitions for students: sentence, paragraph, dialogue, chronological, flashback, internal monologue, heading, numbered list, checklist, journal entry.
Discuss: Text Structure in
Look Both Ways
Prompt students to analyze and discuss the author’s use of text structures in
Look Both Ways
Say:

Think back to the vignettes you have read and identify any structural choices that stand out, such as lists, flashbacks, multiple points of view, or other unusual features. Be ready to explain not just what the structure is, but how it affects what the reader learns about the character.
Ask:
Which of them has unusual text structures? How would you describe them?

“How to Look (Both) Both Ways” jumps back and forth between Fatima’s story and her ongoing checklist of what has changed and what is the same. “Five Things Easier to Do Than Simeon’s and Kenzi’s Secret Handshake” tells Simeon and Kenzi’s story by listing those five things and explaining each one. “Satchmo’s Master Plan” uses flashbacks and a written plan to show where Satchmo’s fear of dogs came from.
Ask:
How do these text structures affect what we learn about the characters and how their stories unfold?

In “Five Things Easier to Do Than Simeon’s and Kenzi’s Secret Handshake,” each of the five things shows us a different character’s point of view. We learn how teachers see the boys, how they see their neighborhood, how they see Fredo, and how Fredo sees them. We learn how important their neighborhood is to Simeon and Kenzi and why they consider themselves to be brothers.
Support students in naming structural elements precisely (list/flashback/alternating sections) and explaining how those choices shape what readers learn about characters and how readers feel.
Require one structural term in every spoken answer (opening/shift/flashback/list/return/ending).
Model one “because” explanation using a concrete example (Fatima’s list; Satchmo’s flashback; Five Things list).
Add precision connectors: as a result, therefore, in contrast.
“The vignette opens with ___, which sets up ___ for the reader.”
“The shift to ___ changes the reader’s understanding because ___.”
“The ending returns to ___ so the reader realizes ___.”
“This structure highlights ___, which helps readers infer ___.”
Normalize multiple valid interpretations: different readers can feel different effects if they cite the structural evidence clearly.
Introduce a simple structure-to-effect routine: structure move → what it highlights → reader effect.
Revoice “it makes it interesting” → “The structure creates tension/curiosity because ___.”
Upgrade “we learn more” → “The structure reveals ___ by ___.”
If students describe plot only → Prompt: “Name the structure move (list/flashback), and tell its effect.”
If students can’t name effect → Prompt: “Does it build tension, show change, or reveal perspective? Choose one.”
Students name a structural element accurately.
Students link structure to character understanding or reader experience.
Students use one connector (because/as a result/in contrast).
Teacher Tip

You may want to prepare a brief summary of each vignette to help jog students’ memories of each one. Include main characters and major plot points as well as the vignette’s structure, especially if it’s more unique.

Struggling with: Recognizing a text’s structure

Scaffold the process of recognizing structure by asking questions. Ex. “Does this story go in chronological order, or does it jump back and forth in time?” “Does this story have just one narrator?” “Does it include other points of view?” “Does it have structural elements like dialogue, letters, lists, or journal entries?”
Ready for extension: Choosing text structure
Ask:

Remember that at the end of this unit, you’ll write your own personal narrative about an “ordinary moment” in your life. Can you think of an interesting type of structure you might use to help tell your story? I might include texts to my friends as part of the story when I am describing the “ordinary moment.” I might include some of my internal thoughts in italics.
Pulse Check (RL.6.5)
How does the ending of “How to Look (Both) Both Ways” fit into its overall structure?
It tells a story outside of Fatima’s list for the first time to contrast her thoughts with what actually happens.
Incorrect: The story outside of Fatima’s list comes in between entries of the list so we can see how events change her list.
It introduces Fatima’s list for the first time to show how the story affected her.
Incorrect: Fatima’s list is introduced at the beginning of the story. The author comes back to it again at the end.
It contrasts Fatima’s story of walking home from school with the silliness of writing lists.
Incorrect: Fatima’s list is part of her daily walk, and the narrator does not make it seem silly.
It returns to Fatima’s list to show how the events of the story affected her.
Correct: The story shares Fatima’s list, describes experiences she has along the way, and returns to the list to show what has changed for her.
Part B: Structure in
Look Both Ways
(RL.6.5, SL.6.1) (20 minutes)
Have students work in three groups, one for each vignette with an unusual structure. If this makes group size unmanageable, two groups may be assigned to each vignette.
Jigsaw Reading

Hand out copies of the 3 Column Chart graphic organizer. Label (or have students label) the three columns: “Vignette Title and Structural Element,” “What It Shows,” and “What I Learned About the Character.”
Say these Directions:

Work with your group to reread your assigned vignette and analyze how its structure affects the story. As you read, identify important structural elements, explain what they show, and record what they help you understand about the character.

Explain that each group will fill out this chart about one vignette with an unusual structure. Each group will then share their thoughts and learn from each other. Briefly model summarizing your thoughts on a story’s structural elements.

Assign each group to one of three vignettes identified as having an unusual structure: “How to Look (Both) Both Ways,” “Five Things Easier to Do Than Simeon’s and Kenzi’s Secret Handshake,” and “Satchmo’s Master Plan.” Invite groups to discuss the following question before completing their graphic organizer.
Say these Directions:

First, summarize how your vignette is organized. Then look closely at how that structure shapes the way information is revealed and how it helps readers understand the character more deeply. Be sure to include at least one specific example from the text.
Ask:
How would you summarize the structure of this vignette?

“Five Things Easier to Do Than Simeon’s and Kenzi’s Secret Handshake” lists five different things that Simeon and Kenzi do after school together, ending with their secret handshake. Each of the five things is numbered and written in paragraph form. These five things show how other characters view Simeon and Kenzi. “Satchmo’s Master Plan” includes a section with his plan that is written in italics and with different paragraph indentations.

Give students time to closely reread and analyze their assigned vignette with their group, annotating the text as needed to record their analysis of the text’s structure and its effects on the reader.
Say:

Closely reread your vignette with your group. Pay attention to the story’s structure, and record your thoughts in the graphic organizer. Remember that your group will need to share your findings with the other groups.
Vignette Title and Structural Element
What It Shows
What I Now Know About the Character
“How to Look (Both) Both Ways,” list
A view inside Fatima’s head
Benni has influenced Fatima enough to change her mind.
“Five Things Easier to Do Than Simeon’s and Kenzi’s Secret Handshake,” five things
Different points of view
I know how people see Simeon and Kenzi and how they see their neighborhood.
“Satchmo’s Master Plan,” flashback
Satchmo’s fears
I understand where his fears came from and how he came up with his plan.
Have one representative from each group share their findings with the other groups. Invite other groups to take notes so each has a completed graphic organizer.
Ask:
What new information did you learn from another group’s summary?

I learned that “Five Things Easier to Do Than Simeon’s and Kenzi’s Secret Handshake” not only shows the boys’ points of view about people (and those people’s points of view about them) but also shows how the boys feel about the neighborhood itself.
Help students write and speak evidence-based evaluations of structure by citing a structural feature + a specific text moment and explaining the effect on character development and reader experience.
Before group reread, set the expectation: each group must bring one structural element + one quoted or paraphrased moment + one effect statement.
During share-out, require a “what I now know” sentence that names character understanding (not just plot).
Encourage groups to compare: “In contrast to ___, this vignette uses ___, which makes the reader ___.”
Push evidence integration: “This line/section shows ___, which suggests ___.”
“The structural element ___ (list/flashback/numbered sections) shows ___ by ___.”
“A specific moment is ___; this makes the reader ___ because ___.”
“What I now know about the character is ___, based on ___.”
“Unlike ___, this vignette uses ___, which changes ___.”
Allow students to choose the evidence format they can access most easily (quote OR precise paraphrase) while still requiring the structure term + effect.
Revoice “it shows her thoughts” → “The list structure reveals her internal perspective by ___.”
Upgrade “it helps” → “It clarifies/complicates/shifts the reader’s view because ___.”
If evidence is too vague (“somewhere it says . . .”) → Prompt: “Name the section/structural part (opening/ending/list item #), and paraphrase 6–10 words.”
If effect is generic (“it’s better”) → Prompt: “Choose one: tension, humor, empathy, clarity, surprise—then explain why.”
Students use at least one structure term accurately.
Students cite a specific moment (quote or precise paraphrase).
Students explain an effect on reader experience and what we learn about a character.

Struggling with: Explaining the effects of structure

Ask questions to help scaffold the process of describing the effects of the story’s structure on the reader, characters, etc. Ex. “What do we learn about Fatima when we see her list the first time? What do we learn when we read about what happens to her on the way home? How does that change the list when we see it the second time?”
Ready for extension: Explaining the effects of structure
Ask:

How would the vignette you analyzed be different if it didn’t have a variety of structural elements? What might it lose? If Satchmo’s story just explained how he got attacked by a dog in the past instead of using a flashback, we would know what happened, but we might not understand what a powerful effect it had on him and why he’s still thinking about it years later.

By the end of the year, read and comprehend literature, including stories, dramas, and poems, in the grades 6–8 text complexity band proficiently, with scaffolding as needed at the high end of the range.
